Stated Claim / Post Context:
Flydubai Captain: Co-Pilot Asked to Pray, Then Struck Him With Axe — Al-Qaeda Propaganda Calls for More Attacks

The captain of the Flydubai jet targeted in Wednesday’s attempted hijacking said his co-pilot asked to pray just minutes before striking him from behind with a cockpit crash axe, as new evidence revealed the suspect’s apparent affinity for al-Qaeda and pro-al-Qaeda propaganda calling for further attacks on aircraft carrying Americans and Israelis.
The post Flydubai Captain: Co-Pilot Asked to Pray, Then Struck Him With Axe — Al-Qaeda Propaganda Calls for More Attacks appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
The captain of the Flydubai jet targeted in Wednesday’s attempted hijacking said his co-pilot asked to pray just minutes before striking him from behind with a cockpit crash axe, as new evidence revealed the suspect’s apparent affinity for al-Qaeda and pro-al-Qaeda propaganda calling for further attacks on aircraft carrying Americans and Israelis.

Captain Smit Machchhar, who was badly wounded during the attack aboard Flydubai Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, gave his most detailed account yet of the ordeal Saturday in a conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

“It was a normal flight,” Machchhar said, recalling that his co-pilot, 29-year-old Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, told him that he wanted to pray.

Machchhar said the request did not initially strike him as unusual and that he turned forward out of respect.

“Suddenly, after four or five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head,” he said.

“My first thought was that there was catastrophic damage to the aircraft,” Machchhar continued. “But after that, the blows kept coming, one after the other. That’s when I realized it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

The United Arab Emirates’ attorney general revealed Saturday that Hammami had armed himself with the Boeing 737 MAX’s cockpit crash axe — an emergency tool kept aboard commercial aircraft — and attacked Machchhar before attempting to seize the flight controls in what Emirati authorities formally described as an attempted “terrorist attack.”

Badly injured and with his vision blurred by repeated blows to the head, Machchhar said he then felt the aircraft “sharply going down.”

He initially tried to open the cockpit door but was stopped by Hammami, who was also preventing crew members outside from entering with the door’s access code. Lying on the cockpit floor as he heard screams from the cabin, Machchhar said he summoned what strength he had left for one final attempt.

“I had one last fight left in me,” he said. “If I don’t do it, I’m going to die.”

Machchhar lunged for the door and managed to open it.

“People were waiting to pounce back, and take control, and the rest is what you know, sir,” he told Netanyahu.

Israeli passengers rushed the cockpit, with passenger Yaniv Hayun grabbing Hammami by the neck and pulling him away from the controls as others restrained him. Hayun briefly helped stabilize the aircraft before off-duty pilots aboard the flight took over and ultimately brought the badly damaged jet down safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

As investigators reconstruct what happened inside the cockpit, new evidence is also emerging about Hammami’s apparent affinity for al-Qaeda.

CNN reported Saturday that accounts bearing Hammami’s name featured footage of Israeli aircraft alongside images of prominent al-Qaeda figures.

One video, filmed in part from the cockpit of a Boeing 737 MAX at Dubai International Airport, zoomed in on an El Al aircraft before ending with images of Ayman al-Zawahiri, Osama bin Laden’s successor as al-Qaeda leader, and Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi, an al-Qaeda loyalist whose 2009 suicide bombing in Afghanistan killed seven CIA personnel and two others.

The video was posted to Hammami’s LinkedIn account roughly nine hours after Wednesday’s attack, when Hammami was already in custody. CNN said it could not determine who published the material or whether it had been scheduled in advance. The same videos reportedly appeared around the same time on an Instagram account bearing his name before that account was deleted.

Separate reporting by the Telegraph found more than 2,000 posts from a social media account strongly linked to Hammami dating to 2021 and 2022, including repeated endorsements of violence against women, severe religious punishments, and other extremist rhetoric.

The disclosures come as pro-al-Qaeda propaganda is openly celebrating the Flydubai attack and calling for further attacks on aircraft carry
